title.en: The Orphans and the Seal-Skin Disguise
title.zh: 孤兒姊弟與海豹皮偽裝

region.en: Winter settlement on the islets, Greenland

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 29 'The Orphans', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Shut into an empty house by stone while the settlement moves off, the starving orphans bore through the roof, eat winter leavings, and — remembering their mother's magic songs — the sister rubs a thong-seal skin until it wraps the brother whole: he plays seal in the calm, and the unjacketed kayakers who chase him sink in the storm he sings up. Taken in, then fed a knee-pan as first bite by a new master, he grows strong; years later he makes the old man choose between a knee-pan and boiling train-oil — the scald kills him drinking — and the appeased orphan leaves on the first thaw.
summary.zh: 村民遷徙時用巨石封門，將姊弟二人鎖入空屋。饑餓中他們鑿穿屋頂而出，靠殘食度日；妹妹憶起母親所授咒歌，把長鬚海豹皮揉唱到能將弟弟整個裹住——他扮作小海豹引來追獵，唱起風暴咒，未著防水衣的皮艇客盡數翻沉。被收留後又被主人罰吞膝蓋骨；數年後他長成壯漢，回敬那老者：『吞膝骨容易，還是喝滾油容易？請您試試。』滾油燙喉，老者當場斃命，姊弟於初融時離去。

sensitivity.note: Rink's note lists related orphan fragments (ptarmigan-and-seals gifts, the fire that could never be extinguished, the orphan who walked on the ocean). Scalding death recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: In a well-peopled settlement there lived an old couple with an only son and a younger daughter; but the parents died before they were grown up. They soon got foster-parents, but these did not love them — always scolded, left to seek their food on the beach at low-water. One spring, when the people were going to start on their summer travels, they put the children into an empty house with a small portion of food, closed the entrance with large stones, and then left them. When the poor orphans were wellnigh starving, they rummaged about the empty room and fell to eating all the old leavings they could get hold of; when these were finished, the sister found an instrument for boring. As they could not reach the ceiling, they heaped up stones to stand upon, and in this way managed to make a hole in the roof to creep through — the brother first helping his sister to escape, then getting out himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 29 'The Orphans'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Outside they could see tents standing in rows on the islets, themselves on the mainland; by the smoke they knew the people to be cooking all the day, and could see the kayakers pursuing the seals. Hungry, they went to the place where the seals used to be stripped in the winter, hoping to find old bits, and were fortunate enough to find the head of a small thong-seal. Having eaten a part of it, the sister stripped off the skin, prepared it, and said to the brother: 'I am going to make a disguise for thee; dost not thou remember the magic song our mother taught us?' 'Indeed I do; and I even remember one for raising a storm. Make haste and get ready the skin.' She rubbed it hard, singing over it, and all the while it grew larger and larger; he tried it on — it only touched his knees — she rubbed still more, and at last he could wrap himself quite up in it. 'There, thou lookest just like a young thong-seal; now try the water' — he leapt down while she remained singing the magic lay, and when he reappeared she sang again, until at last: 'Well, now, thou art quite like a thong-seal; come!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 29 'The Orphans'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning, fine weather and quite calm, and no kayaker from the islets having left land, he took a fancy to play the seal: putting on his disguise he leapt into the sea, and no sooner was he observed from the tents than they called out, 'There is a young seal; let us be off and chase it!' — plenty of joking and a great bustle, the men getting their kayaks down into the sea in a great hurry. In the meantime he dived; as he could not keep his breath all the time, he rose to the surface behind one of the kayakers and took breath without being observed. In the hurry of the moment some of the men had forgotten to put on their kayak-jackets, though rather far out at sea — these the disguised boy had picked out to wreak his vengeance on. He sang the lay for raising the wind, and all of a sudden a gale began to blow; the hunters hastened to put back and reach home, but those who were not in proper trim had their kayaks filled with water and perished.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 29 'The Orphans'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the brother came on shore he said to his sister: 'I believe we may safely venture to let them see we are still alive. Now they have lost some of their people, we may probably be of some use to them, and may be they will fetch us off' — and they made signs to attract attention. As soon as the people on the opposite islands observed them they said to one another, 'Let us get them over; we are in want of people' — a boat despatched, the orphans recovered. Later in the summer they were taken into a boat's crew as rowers and went up a firth for a deer-hunting station; but their master was not kind to them, and when he had got his first buck he gave the boy the knee-pan, saying, 'Until thou hast swallowed that, thou shalt have nothing else to eat' — almost choked, he managed to make it go down, then had his meal, but never forgot the knee-pan. When the deer-hunting was at an end in the autumn, some people were leaving for the north, the orphans among their party, thus leaving their former masters. Not yet quite grown up, they went on practising all manner of hard exercise to increase their strength, and both succeeded — the brother turning out to be an excellent seal-hunter besides. Some years afterwards they travelled back to the south and again came across the man who had made him swallow the knee-pan, now grown quite old. Game was scarce in the middle of winter, but the young man still went out and tried his luck, one day bringing home a large thong-seal, ordering the sister to boil down the blubber into train-oil. This done, he invited all their neighbours; when the meal was served up he addressed the old man: 'I would like to know whether it be easier to swallow a knee-pan or to drink boiling-hot oil? Just thou try, or otherwise thou wilt have no supper.' The old man hesitated, but drank it off at last; his throat got scalded, and he died in the act of drinking. The young man was thus appeased, and left the place on the first thaw.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 29 'The Orphans'; not verbatim.

title.en: Alekatokak, Who Went Away in Search of Her Brother

region.en: Inland valley of shadows and the northern camping plain
region.zh: 幽影之谷與北方營地草原

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; from two rather defective copies, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 30 'The Girl who went away in search of her Brother', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Blamed for her brother Asuvina's disappearance, Alekatokak flees her father's death-threat inland — past a giant who would not let her off, through a house of invisible shadows that feed her, to the camp where a kayaker tows a seal: 'Asuvina has got a seal!' Hidden from the clairvoyant idiot, she watches the chief crush his own feet with the lifting-stone and cures him with a young deer's entrails; married there, she swallows fox-entrails with shut eyes at her son's birth — the custom for clever children — and her boy grows a very swift runner, the family's descendants numerous in the place.
summary.zh: 兄長阿蘇維納失蹤，父親卻揚言要懲罰妹妹阿蕾卡托卡克；她攜衣物袋遠走內陸——躲過揚言不放她走的巨人，被一屋看不見的幽影留宿餵飯，終於在海邊營地聽見孩子們高喊『阿蘇維納獵到海豹啦！』。她藏身避開先知的白痴，眼看酋長舉圓石砸了自己雙腳，便疾奔追回幼鹿、以鹿腸為他療傷；在當地成婚生子，依習俗閉眼吞下狐腸——孩子長成飛毛腿，子孫繁衍於斯。

sensitivity.note: The place of shadows and the fox-entrails birth custom are documented as told; Rink notes the copies are defective.

passages.text: Alekatokak went away with her brother Asuvina to set up fox-traps. Having arrived at the place they had fixed upon, she told her brother that she wanted a flat stone to make a door for the trap, and asked him to bring her one; he went to get it, but as he was rather long in returning she went off to seek him — in vain; he had completely disappeared, and she was obliged to return by herself. On her coming home her father said, 'I suppose thou hast hurt him — perhaps even killed him: I shall be sure to punish thee.' He had often threatened to make away with her, having never liked her, but put her down as an idle wench, unable to make herself useful in any way. Her mother pitied her, and advised her to flee the society of men; accordingly she made up a little bag with some clothes, and went far into the country, wandering about, and could even overtake the reindeer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 30 'The Girl who went away in search of her Brother'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Having once passed a cleft in the mountains, she saw a little house down in a valley, with an opening in the centre of the roof; peeping down she observed a giant-like fellow, who returned the look and addressed her: 'What dost thou want here, thou miserable daughter of the coast-people? Dost thou think that I will let thee off like that?' He rushed out to seize her, but meanwhile she had found a hiding-place; when he had returned to his house she again hastened on farther into the country, and at last came to another house, which had three windows. She noticed that cooking was going on inside, as well as other business, without any people being visible — though not aware of it, she had been coming all the way to the place of shadows. A voice was heard saying, 'Thou little one from the coast-side, come in, come in!' — and when she had entered, a dish with boiled meat was set before her; her hunger stilled, the invisible shadows invited her to stay and sleep there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 30 'The Girl who went away in search of her Brother'; not verbatim.

passages.text: After farther wanderings she at length reached the sea, and around a little creek observed a great many tents pitched up near the strand; waiting till evening before venturing down, she sat on a slope and heard the children of the place call out, 'A kayaker is coming! he is towing a seal!' — presently a kayaker appeared from behind a point, and they repeated, 'Asuvina has got a seal!' — and she felt sure she had found her lost brother. The people of the place had a chief whose tent was larger than all the rest, and beyond this a plain where they used to practise ball-playing; she recognised her brother accompanying the men thither, and saw that he was ordered to lift up a large round stone — not being able, the others threw him down. In the evening she descended the hill and went straight to his house; he wondered very much at her coming, told her he had lost his way in seeking the slab for her fox-trap, but was now married, his wife having a sister. There was an idiot at the place who, by clairvoyance, would probably soon be aware of her arrival — she had better hide herself a while behind the skin-hangings of the wall. Next morning the fool entered, saying, 'In the night I dreamt that a woman from the coast-side, and sister to Asuvina, came among us'; but Asuvina answered, 'I have got no sister' — and the other went away; Asuvina stayed at home the whole day long, enjoying his sister's company.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 30 'The Girl who went away in search of her Brother'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the evening she went with them to the ball-play on the plain, disguised in the clothes of her sister-in-law. When the chief had lifted the round stone he made a false hit, and let it fall down upon his own feet, and fairly crushed them. Alekatokak now told them quickly to fetch a little dog; but on hearing that they had not got one in the whole place, she hurried away and soon overtook and brought back a young deer; she cut an opening into it, and let the chief put the sore feet down among the entrails, and in this way cured him. She got married there and had a son; at his birth they brought her an oblong dish with certain entrails of a fox, and ordered her to swallow them, shutting her eyes the while — this was the custom with them when they desired the new-born child to be clever and dexterous. After this remedy she was at once restored to her usual health, and her boy grew to be a very swift runner; and they remained in the place and had numerous descendants.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 30 'The Girl who went away in search of her Brother'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Dog: Origin of the Howling at the Last Point
title.zh: 狗：吠送行舟之俗的由來

region.zh: 海岸聚落與內陸人營地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; single manuscript, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 31 'The Dog', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Nursed at the ledge with her own milk after the inlanders hang her sons on an inaccessible rock, a mother adopts a magic whelp that scratches its face and asks 'What do I look like now?' — its scratching a charm to frighten people to death. It frightens a whole conjuring-house dead, fetches storehouse victuals to the starving family, and is abandoned when the boat sails, following along the shore to whine and howl at the last point — the origin, the teller says, of the dogs that follow the departing boat along the coast and go on howling at them from the last point of land.
summary.zh: 內陸人把兩個兒子倒吊於不可攀的危崖上；悲憤的母親領回一只有靈的狗崽，以乳汁哺於長凳之上。狗兒抓著自己的臉問『我現在好看嗎？』——那抓撓正是嚇死人的咒術。它使一座降神屋的人當場嚇死，又為絕糧的一家搬回存糧。開春船隻啟航時，母親藉口讓它回屋取物，隨即解纜而去；狗沿岸追至最後一處岬角，再無路可走，唯有對著船嗚咽長嚎——今日狗群追船吠送之俗，即由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Etiological ending documented in the source. The hanged sons and fright-killing recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: An old married couple had two sons and a little daughter; the sons were renowned for strength and for being able hunters, used to return with their seals towing in a long line behind them — but one day they did not return. While the parents were still expecting them, a man brought the sad news that he had seen them both hanging on an inaccessible rock, hung up by the feet, head downwards, nobody able to get at them to save them; this deed had been done by the inlanders. While the old parents were in deep affliction for their loss, they heard that some of their neighbours had a dog with a great many whelps; the mother sent the daughter away to fetch one, which she adopted, and had it always on the ledge beside her, nursing it with her own milk. In the winter she noticed that the dog, being endowed with magic power, sometimes went on scratching his face, and at the same time always commencing to speak, asking, 'What do I look like now?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 31 'The Dog'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Towards the end of the winter they were in great want, having lost their protectors. The dog then said he was going for a walk into the country; one night he roused his foster-mother, and having given himself a scratching, inquired, 'Am I still good-looking? I shall be off to-morrow' — the reason for thus scratching itself was to frighten people to death by charm. He came upon the inlanders while they were busy conjuring spirits; the angakok soon foretold his coming, and cried, 'Fire! fire!' but the dog scratched his face and rushed into the passage, hiding itself there; when the people came out, bringing lights with them, the dog frightened them to death on the spot. Next he set off in search of their storehouse, and carried some victuals back to his foster-parents, showing them the place where they could find the rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 31 'The Dog'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But from that time upwards the woman began to fear him; and in the spring, when the boat was loaded and ready for starting, she asked the dog to go back to the house and bring her something she had forgotten. As soon as it had disappeared to obey her orders, they pushed off from land and set out on their journey. The dog went on following along the shore until they gained the last point, from which it could follow them no longer; there it remained whining and howling. It is supposed that this is the origin of the present custom with the dogs to follow the departing boat along the coast, and go on howling at them from the last point of land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 31 'The Dog'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Widow's Vengeance: The Bear and the Poisoned Loin
title.zh: 寡婦復仇記：靈熊與咒肉

region.en: Iceberg grounds and rival household, Greenland coast
region.zh: 格陵蘭冰山海面與仇家屋舍

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; one of the older manuscripts, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 32 'The Widow's Vengeance', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Refused even a taviorasak of blubber, the widow charms an eider-duck, a small seal, and at last a completely furnished kayak into being; her son Kujanguak climbs the iceberg the brothers could not and flings down a bear stone-dead. When they set on him on the water, the sea-water-charm loosens their grip; across the breakers he rides the surf. A spelled piece of loin kills Sanak at the shared feast; the eldest shakes the house-pillars and tears off her jacket-points, but the widow, her back broken leaping the boat, flings the filth of her dead mother's corner at the enemies' house — sickness kills them all but the sister, who turns kivigtok.
summary.zh: 討一點油脂也被拒的寡婦，以咒術接連變出海雀、小海豹，乃至一艘配備齊全的皮艇；其子庫江瓜克登上連兄弟們都攀不上的冰山，把熊活活摔死海中。兄弟們在水上圍攻他，他蘸一口海水便令其鬆手，又踏浪越過碎浪帶。分肉的宴席上，一小塊被咒的腰肉使三納克窒息而死；長兄搖撼屋柱、撕她衣角，寡婦卻在跳船時折了背——臨終前她將亡母角落裡的穢物擲向仇家之屋，瘟疫隨之而至，唯其妹遁入內陸為奇維托克人。

sensitivity.note: Charm-made objects (duck, seal, kayak) and corpse-filth sorcery documented as told in the 1875 source. Multiple deaths recorded.

passages.text: There was a widow with a son named Kujanguak; beyond her house was another one, inhabited by a number of brothers, all clever at their profession and well off. Whenever they had brought home any seals, the widow, according to the custom, would send her son to get a taviorasak (little bit of blubber); but the men generally replied, 'Thou lazy beggar, thou never assisted us in providing anything; so thou wilt not get anything neither.' On his returning with this answer his mother only said, 'Never mind — just let them talk.' One day they caught a mamartok (a delicious kind of seal that has shed hair); the mother now took a stronger fancy than ever for a little morsel, and sent her son for it — he was treated as usual: the men took a bit of whatever they could lay hand on and flung it at him. When he came back and gave their message to his mother, she was in a great rage; taking one of her boots, she seated herself in a corner of the ledge to practise some charm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 32 'The Widow's Vengeance'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the following morning, when her son looked into the pot, there was an eider-duck in it — 'Just take it' — part boiled, the rest put by for future use. In the evening she repeated her charms and spells, and a small seal was found in the water-tub. The third day, the son, to his great surprise, saw standing on the floor a completely furnished kayak; the mother took him down to the beach, and made him practise paddling, as well as upsetting and again righting, till he had got quite expert at these things. The following day she let him go out again, and pointing to an iceberg told him to round it in his kayak; the neighbours likewise set off, and saw Kujanguak attacking a bear, which at last took refuge on an iceberg. The eldest of the brothers tried to climb it, but was not able; after him Kujanguak made the attempt — having first asked the other to take care of his kayak, he clutched hold of the ice and scrambled up. At the very top he encountered the bear, and immediately fell upon it; taking hold of it by the neck, he flung it down into the sea, stone-dead. The youngest of the brothers, Sanak, cried out, 'I have got a bear!' — but Kujanguak quietly descended, got into his kayak, fastened his towing-line to the bear, and paddled home, followed by the other kayakers who had given him their assistance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 32 'The Widow's Vengeance'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The mother went down to the beach accompanied by the sister of the brothers; while they were busy dragging the bear up to the house the mother mockingly observed, turning to her, 'Who knows how nourishing that flesh may be!' adding, 'Now haul it up the rest of the way thyself; I am going to fetch water.' Having finished this task, however, she returned to the bear, divided it into two equal parts, and gave her companion one: 'The skin thou mayst keep for a ledge-cover.' She boiled the flesh and invited the whole party to partake of it, seating the other woman on the main ledge; when she had served the meal up she remarked, 'It is a pity one cannot make sure whether there is any nourishment about this game of Kujanguak's' — the visitor said she had been longing ever so much for bear's meat lately, they all ate well, and on taking leave the female visitor thanked her, saying she had altogether found it a delicious and hearty feed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 32 'The Widow's Vengeance'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The following day Kujanguak again set off to the iceberg and got a large seal; returning towing it homewards, he chanced to encounter the brothers — happily his mother had advised him beforehand, 'If ever they venture to persecute thee, take some water out of the sea with thy left hand, and moisten thy lips with it.' He tried this as soon as they all came rushing in upon him; the eldest brother began the attack by catching hold of the kayak point, doing his utmost to upset it — no sooner had Kujanguak tasted the water with his lips than the other let it go. 'Look at the foaming breakers there! let us try which of us can first get beyond them' — all pushed on as fast as possible; Kujanguak, who had a seal on his line, was first obliged to tighten it, but this done, pushed on like a shot and soon came up with the eldest brother ahead of the others; while they rowed outside of the breakers, Kujanguak went right across them, carried along by the surf. When the waves retreated he jumped out upon the rocks; when the breakers came rolling on again, he hastened back into the kayak. On the way home the brothers secretly consulted to surround him; however, he made his escape from them. Meanwhile his mother suddenly missed a certain lock of hair, knowing this to be a bad omen for her son, very anxious about him until it shortly afterwards proved to be in its proper place on her forehead; reassured, she mounted the hills to look out for his return. On landing he was received on the beach by her along with the other woman, who asked him how her brothers had fared — 'I wonder thou carest to bother thyself about those stupid fellows!' When the flesh of the seal had been prepared and the men were supping upon the briskets, the mother of the many sons grew envious and resentful because she was not invited to share the good fare; on hearing this the widow cut a piece of the loin, and having pronounced a spell upon it, carried it to her by way of a present. When they sat down to eat it, Sanak was almost suffocated, and presently his old mother likewise cried for water — having got a drink she recovered; Sanak, however, expired. When the widow re-entered the room, the eldest brother accused her of the deed: 'You only fed them to work their destruction — it is none but thou who hast killed them!' — and rose and rushed against the house-pillars to shake it down and make it fall over her; but the widow replaced them quickly. Again he rose from his seat, and turning towards the widow herself, quickly snatched off the two points of her jacket, the one in front as well as the one behind. Little heeding this affront, she now ran out and told her son that two of their adversaries had now been despatched; in the enjoyment of the happy event they both bolted across the boat in great glee — however, the mother happened to break her back. When Kujanguak had got her indoors, she took some filth from beneath the place where her dead mother used to put all kinds of dirty refuse, and threw it out at the house of their enemies; this brought sickness upon them, from which all of them died excepting the sister, who turned kivigtok.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 32 'The Widow's Vengeance'; not verbatim.

title.en: A Lamentable Story: The Cleft That Closed
title.zh: 悲慘的故事：合攏的石縫

region.en: Rock cleft by the sealing ice, Greenland
region.zh: 格陵蘭獵豹冰畔的石縫

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; one of the older manuscripts, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 33 'A Lamentable Story', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: One shout from playing children, carrying their baby sisters and brothers in their hoods, spoils an old man's seal — and in his rage he cries 'Shut up, mountain-cleft!' — and it closes upon all of them, wide at the bottom, narrow at the top. The babies cry for thirst; the girls suck their fingers and hush them — 'When mother has finished soling the boots, she will come and suckle thee.' The mothers come and pour water down the cleft, trickling along the walls to be licked up, see the children plainly, and cannot get at them — and all of them are starved.
summary.zh: 孩子們背著兜帽中的弟妹在石縫間嬉戲，一聲歡呼驚走了老人的海豹。他盛怒喝道：『合上吧，山縫！』石縫應聲閉合，將孩子們全部困於底闊頂窄的巖窟之中。嬰兒啼哭要水，女孩們把手指塞進他們嘴裡哄道：『等媽媽補好靴底，就來餵你了。』母親們趕來，把水沿縫灌下，孩子們沿壁舔飲；母親們看得清清楚楚，卻無法救出——孩子們終究全數餓死。

sensitivity.note: Same motif family as Rasmussen's 'The man who became a star' (Nalaussartoq, cross-ref inuit-man-became-star); here without the star transformation. Child deaths recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: An old man had taken up his position on the ice watching the breathing-holes of the seals, in order to spear them as they appeared. Meanwhile some little girls were playing on shore in a cleft between some rocks, as usual, carrying their little baby sisters and brothers in the amowts (hoods) at their backs. Just as the old man was in the act of spearing a seal, the children happened to give a shout, and the terrified seal at once dived to the bottom. On this the old man got into a great passion, and cried out aloud, 'Shut up, mountain-cleft!' — and accordingly it closed upon all the playing children, who were not able to escape, but were now buried in a cavern, wide at the bottom, and narrow towards the top.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 33 'A Lamentable Story'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The babies soon began to cry for thirst, and the girls put their fingers into their mouths to suck at, trying to hush them by telling them, 'When mother has finished soling the boots, she will come and suckle thee.' At length the mothers came to the spot, and poured water down in the cleft; the water trickled along the walls, and they licked it up, and the mothers could very well see the children, but as it was impossible to get at them, all of them were starved.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 33 'A Lamentable Story'; not verbatim.
